Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Arabidopsis RCD1 Coordinates Chloroplast and Mitochondrial Functions through Interaction with ANAC Transcription Factors" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Christian Hardtke (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and two reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved, but the reviewers are of the opinion that you did not adequately respond to key requests from the first round of reviews. We would thus like to ask you to carefully consider the reviews pasted below, and revise your manuscript accordingly.

Reviewer #1:

In this revised version the authors addressed many small and large issues raised by the reviewers and editor. However, I feel some of the main concerns have not been addressed appropriately yet.

The authors try to introduce a new mechanism of how RCD1 directly binds and inhibits ANAC017/13. This possibly interaction represses the transcription factors and thus would keep MRR target gene expression under control, such as AOX1a. Upon oxidative stress, RCD1 aggregates and would then release some of the ANAC017/13 to induce MRR gene expression. This interesting model has a number of testable implications, which were suggested after initial review, and were also underlined to be important by the Editor. However some of these have not been addressed directly.

1) In comment by eLife Senior Editor: "One important experiment would be to look for suppression of NAC17-dependent retrograde signalling in an RCD overexpression and/or RCD 7cys complemented line. Notably, these lines should be readily available, and as such these are not very challenging experiments."

And reviewer 2 "To make this more convincing, more direct experiments should be performed. One would for instance expect that an RCD1 Overexpression line (which has been made in the past, Fujibe 2006, Biosci. Biotechnol. Biochem., 70 (8), 1827-1831, and complements the rcd1 MV resistance phenotype) would suppress (AA-induced) MRR to a significant extent. The 7cys RCD1 line would also be of interest in this context, to show that redox state can affect retrograde signalling."

The authors respond in point 1 that a number of rcd1 RCD1-HA with higher and lower levels of RCD1 (thus probably equivalent to an RCD1 overexpression line, but hard to say without RCD1 specific antibody, and only an anti-HA antibody) have been generated. The authors then show the MV-dependent Fv/Fm phenotype is reverting to different extents to Col-0. This is nice, but the key experiment to address the raised question is then missing. When treated with a Mitochondrial Retrograde Regulation inducing agent (classically antimycin A), do these “overexpression” lines show a reduction in ANAC017-dependent MRR gene expression (e.g. Aox1a, UPOX, UGT74E2)? The authors did experiments along these lines but using MV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D). MV however does not directly induce mitochondrial signalling as it mainly affects chloroplastic ROS, which is supported by the fact that MRR marker genes AOX1a and UPOX are not induced by MV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D). I don't see why the authors did not do the same experiment using AA, which would address the question, and is relatively easy to perform. In the RCD1d7cys complemented line, which fails to aggregate, such a repression of AA-induction of MRR genes may not occur, and would thus be expected to show more WT-like gene expression responses.

2) A second experiment that was suggested was to use rcd1 mutants complemented with RCD1 lacking the ANAC017 interaction domain (RST domain). In point 3 the authors describe RCD1dRST-HA complementation lines were generated. I assume this is indeed transformation into the rcd1 mutant background, so I suggest these line are called rcd1 RC1dRST-HA in the text and figures (e.g. Figure 7B-C), same for rcd1 RCD1-HA. This to avoid confusion that they are in the Col-0 background, which would lead to a different interpretation. The results in Figure 7B and C are indeed in line with the fact that the RST1 domain is important for RCD1 function in this context. As RCD1 is known to interact with a wide range of transcription factors, so it is not direct evidence for a role via interaction with ANAC017/13, but overall that is a nice result.

3) My comments regarding the size of the aggregates have been addressed.

4) Also the comments regarding Fv/Fm measurement on the rcd1 sal1 have been addressed, it is interesting to see that it shows much higher tolerance to MV than rcd1 itself.

5) I still think it is important to show the visual phenotype of the rcd1 anac017 mutant plants, even if they don't seem to revert the rcd1 ozone resistance phenotype, as is partially observed for the MV Fv/Fm phenotype. This makes some sense, as anac017 is not known to be involved in ozone tolerance.

6) I don't really understand the author's reasoning in point 37 of their reply letter. The authors say there is no effect of AA on RCD1-HA redox state, but Figure 4—figure supplement 2B to me shows induction of higher order complexes by AA and myx of the same size as MV in light or H2O2, albeit weaker. 2.5 μm is a relatively low concentration, as 50 μm AA has been used most extensively throughout the literature. They also say that because MDS gene induction (by which they mean AOX protein level changes using Western blots) by AA is still occurring in rcd1, this leads them to conclude that RCD1 is unlikely part of AA signalling. As RCD1 is suggested to suppress ANAC017 signalling, an rcd1 KO should still show AA gene induction, as the potential repressor is now inactive. An RCD1 OX line may display reduction in AA signalling, but this question has still not been addressed, see Point 1.

Reviewer #2:

The authors have thoroughly revised their previous manuscript version and provide additional evidence for their lines of thoughts and conclusions. The study contributes important and novel information to our understanding of retrograde signaling and the integration of chloroplast and mitochondrial retrograde signals. In the following you find the combined list of minor and very few more critical points.

Introduction section, first paragraph: “… transport of carbon rich metabolites…” It is not really clear what is meant? Carbon rich might be a fatty acid? energy-rich like dihydroxyacetone phosphate or malate?

Introduction section, second paragraph: “… leakage of electrons…”; is this still an adequate description of the process? Our concept of ROS signaling more and more assumes that ROS are generated to enable regulation.

Introduction section, fourth paragraph: “… provides positive feedback regulation”; please be more precise and give the direction:.… provides positive feedback and thus enhancement of the signal.

Subsection “Mitochondrial respiration is altered in rcd1”, opening sentence: I would omit the U here, since it is confusing for the non-expert, and in the legend and Materials and methods it will be mentioned. But in fact the uniformity of label is not explained, is it?

Subsection “Retrograde signaling from both chloroplasts and mitochondria is altered in rcd1”: msh1, recA3 (add comma)

Discussion third: In the same paragraph: “suggests that RCD1 is not a redox sensor of mitochondrial ROS/ redox signaling” still sounds like an overinterpretation of the data and should be toned down. “unlikely is.…” In fact in context with the subsequent discussion, it is not really clear what this statement means. If mitochondrial alterations in metabolism cause redox changes in the nucleus/cytosol similar to those of the chloroplast, then the conformational changes should be the same. The power of mitochondrial redox/ROS signals may just be less than chloroplast redox/ROS signals.

claims.evidence: Supported by chlorophyll fluorescence measurements showing decreased MV tolerance after SHAM treatment (Figure 4E).

claims.claim: Mitochondrial AOXs contribute to resistance of PSII to chloroplastic ROS.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicated that mitochondrial AOXs contributed to resistance of PSII to chloroplastic ROS.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of AOX induction (AA/myx) and inhibition (SHAM) on MV tolerance.

claims.claim: AOX1a isoform is neither sufficient nor necessary for chloroplast ROS tolerance.
claims.source: Noteworthy, analyses of AOX1a-OE, aox1a and rcd1 aox1a lines demonstrated that AOX1a isoform was neither sufficient nor necessary for chloroplast ROS tolerance (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by chlorophyll fluorescence measurements showing no difference in MV tolerance between AOX1a-OE and aox1a, and between rcd1 and rcd1 aox1a (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claims.claim: A pathway in rcd1 links the chloroplast ETC to the activity of mitochondrial AOXs.
claims.source: This hinted that a pathway in rcd1 linked the chloroplast ETC to the activity of mitochondrial AOXs, with the latter functioning as an electron sink.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the increase in Fs after combined MV and SHAM treatment in rcd1 (Figure 5A).

claims.claim: Illumination of MV-pretreated plants leads to dramatic decrease in malate concentration in Col-0, but not in rcd1.

claims.evidence: Supported by metabolite measurements showing different malate levels in Col-0 vs rcd1 after MV treatment in light (Figure 5B).

claims.claim: The activity of NADPH-dependent malate dehydrogenase (NADPH-MDH) is increased in rcd1.
claims.source: Both values were higher in rcd1 than in Col-0 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by enzyme activity measurements showing higher initial and total NADPH-MDH activity in rcd1 (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: The activation state of NADPH-MDH is increased in rcd1.
claims.source: To determine the contribution of in vivo thiol redox state, the initial NADPH-MDH activity was divided by the total activity. This value, the activation state, was also increased in rcd1 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by enzyme activity measurements showing higher activation state in rcd1 (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: Mitochondria contribute to ROS processing in the chloroplasts via a mechanism involving mitochondrial AOXs and possibly the malate shuttle.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggested that mitochondria contributed to ROS processing in the chloroplasts via a mechanism involving mitochondrial AOXs and possibly the malate shuttle.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined effects on AOXs, malate levels, and NADPH-MDH activity.

claims.claim: Transcriptional changes observed in rcd1 show striking similarity to those affected by disturbed organellar function.
claims.source: This revealed a striking similarity of genes differentially regulated in rcd1 to those affected by disturbed organellar function (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by transcriptomic comparison showing overlap between rcd1 and various organellar perturbations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: A significant overlap exists between genes mis-regulated in rcd1 and the mitochondrial dysfunction stimulon (MDS) genes.
claims.source: In particular, a significant overlap was observed between genes mis-regulated in rcd1 and the mitochondrial dysfunction stimulon (MDS) genes (De Clercq et al., 2013) (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Supported by transcriptomic analysis showing overlap between rcd1 and MDS genes (Figure 6A).

claims.claim: SOT12 protein accumulates in rcd1 under standard growth conditions.

claims.evidence: Supported by immunoblotting showing higher SOT12 levels in rcd1 (Figure 6B).

claims.claim: The single sal1 mutant is more tolerant to MV than Col-0.

claims.claim: The ANAC-responsive cis-element is significantly enriched in promoter regions of rcd1 mis-regulated genes.
claims.source: The ANAC-responsive cis-element (De Clercq et al., 2013) was significantly enriched in promoter regions of rcd1 mis-regulated genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the increased MDS expression in rcd1 and the interaction with ANAC factors.

claims.source: Methyl viologen (MV) enhances ROS generation in illuminated chloroplasts by catalyzing the transfer of electrons from Photosystem I (PSI) to molecular oxygen.

claims.source: In illuminated chloroplasts, superoxide anion formed from O2 reduction by Photosystem I (PSI) is converted to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) which is further reduced to water by chloroplastic H2O2-scavenging systems during the water-water cycle (Asada, 2006; Awad et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on the water-water cycle.

claims.claim: H2O2 is involved in many retrograde signaling pathways.

claims.source: Organellar H2O2 has been suggested to translocate directly to the nucleus (Caplan et al., 2015; Exposito-Rodriguez et al., 2017), where it can oxidize thiol groups of specific proteins, thereby converting the ROS signal into thiol redox signals (Møller and Kristensen, 2004; Nietzel et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on H2O2 translocation and signaling.

claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on PAP metabolism.

claims.source: Mitochondrial signaling via ANAC017 was recently suggested to converge with chloroplast PAP signaling based on similarities in their transcriptomic profiles (Van Aken and Pogson, 2017).

claims.source: Under standard growth conditions, the rcd1 mutant displays differential expression of over 400 genes, including those encoding mitochondrial AOXs (Jaspers et al., 2009; Brosché et al., 2014) and the chloroplast 2-Cys peroxiredoxin (2-CP) (Heiber et al., 2007; Hiltscher et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous transcriptomic studies on rcd1.

results.result: The rcd1 mutant exhibits increased tolerance to methyl viologen (MV)-induced photosystem II (PSII) inhibition under light conditions. This tolerance inversely correlates with RCD1 expression levels in complementation lines, suggesting RCD1 quantitatively lowers photosynthetic apparatus resistance to ROS. The increased tolerance is not due to altered MV access to PSI.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 are well-supported by chlorophyll fluorescence measurements (Figure 1A), dose-response analysis in complementation lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and DUAL-PAM measurements showing identical PSI oxidation kinetics (Figure 1B). The data consistently demonstrate that RCD1 negatively regulates tolerance to chloroplastic ROS.

results.result: The chloroplast 2-Cys peroxiredoxin (2-CP) enzyme is maintained in a more reduced state in rcd1 compared to wild-type plants, suggesting RCD1 is involved in regulating the redox status of chloroplastic thiol enzymes.
results.evaluation: Claim C18 is directly supported by thiol bond-specific labeling experiments (Figure 1C) showing predominantly reduced 2-CP in rcd1. Claim C19 is a reasonable inference from this observation, though the mechanism remains to be elucidated.

results.result: ROS treatments alter RCD1 protein abundance, thiol redox state, and oligomerization in vivo. MV and H2O2 treatments cause gradual decrease in RCD1 levels and rapid conversion to high-molecular-weight aggregates. These redox changes occur only in light for MV treatment, indicating chloroplastic ROS mediate the effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 and C20-C22 are well-supported by immunoblotting under reducing conditions (Figure 2A) and non-reducing SDS-PAGE (Figure 2B). The light-dependency of MV-induced changes (Figure 2B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) provides strong evidence for chloroplastic ROS involvement.

results.result: Seven interdomain cysteine residues in RCD1 are involved in regulating protein oligomerization and stability in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is supported by experiments with the RCD1Δ7Cys-HA variant showing reduced aggregation and increased stability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C). However, the functional significance is uncertain since this variant does not alter MV tolerance or gene expression responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).

results.result: The rcd1 mutant displays more active carbohydrate metabolism and higher respiration rate compared to wild-type, indicative of mitochondrial defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by [U-14C] glucose feeding experiments showing increased metabolic fluxes in rcd1 (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1). The increased respiration flux and redistribution of radiolabel to sucrose, starch, and cell wall provide consistent evidence for altered mitochondrial metabolism.

results.result: The rcd1 mutant shows increased abundance and activity of alternative oxidases (AOXs), with elevated AOX capacity dependent on the AOX1a isoform. Multiple AOX isoforms accumulate in rcd1.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 are supported by immunoblotting (Figure 4A), oxygen consumption measurements (Figure 4C), and analysis of the rcd1 aox1a double mutant. The data consistently show elevated AOX levels and activity in rcd1, with AOX1a-dependent respiration capacity.

results.result: Mitochondrial complex III inhibitors (AA, myx) increase PSII resistance to chloroplastic ROS, mimicking the rcd1 phenotype. AOX inhibitor SHAM increases sensitivity to MV in both wild-type and rcd1. However, the AOX1a isoform is neither sufficient nor necessary for chloroplast ROS tolerance.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are well-supported by chlorophyll fluorescence measurements (Figures 4D, 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4). The pharmacological manipulations and genetic analyses with AOX1a-OE, aox1a, and rcd1 aox1a lines provide converging evidence that mitochondrial AOXs (but not specifically AOX1a) contribute to PSII protection.

results.result: A pathway in rcd1 links the chloroplast electron transport chain to mitochondrial AOX activity, possibly involving the malate shuttle. Evidence includes altered chlorophyll fluorescence dynamics, differential malate levels after MV treatment, and increased NADPH-MDH activity and activation state in rcd1.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by chlorophyll fluorescence measurements (Figure 5A), malate quantification (Figure 5B), and NADPH-MDH activity assays (Figure 5C). However, the mechanistic connection remains inferential and would benefit from additional validation experiments.

results.result: Transcriptional changes in rcd1 show striking similarity to genes affected by organellar dysfunction, particularly the mitochondrial dysfunction stimulon (MDS) genes. RCD1 inactivation leads to increased MDS gene expression, elevated SOT12 protein, and severe developmental defects in the rcd1 sal1 double mutant. ANAC-responsive cis-elements are enriched in rcd1 mis-regulated genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by transcriptomic analyses (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), immunoblotting (Figure 6B), phenotypic observations (Figure 6C), MV tolerance assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), and promoter analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The data consistently demonstrate overlap between RCD1 and organellar signaling pathways.

results.result: RCD1 interacts in vivo with ANAC013 and ANAC017 transcription factors. RCD1, SRO1, ANAC013, and ANAC017 are components of the same protein complex in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C45-C48 are well-supported by reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments in Arabidopsis (Table 1, Figure 7—source data 1-2) and co-immunoprecipitation in HEK293T cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The mass spectrometry data provide strong evidence for in vivo complex formation.

results.result: The RCD1 RST domain directly and specifically interacts with ANAC013 in vitro, as demonstrated by NMR spectroscopy showing profound chemical shift changes upon peptide binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 are supported by NMR HSQC spectra (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 3C) and surface plasmon resonance (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B). The data demonstrate specific binding between the RCD1 RST domain and ANAC013 peptide.

results.result: The RCD1 RST domain is necessary for regulating mitochondrial respiration and chloroplast ROS processing. RCD1ΔRST-HA lines show increased AOX accumulation and rcd1-like tolerance to chloroplastic ROS.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 and C59 are supported by immunoblotting (Figure 7B) and chlorophyll fluorescence measurements (Figure 7C) in RCD1ΔRST-HA lines. The data demonstrate that the RST domain-mediated interaction with ANAC factors is functionally important for RCD1's regulatory role.

results.result: RCD1 suppresses ANAC017 activity, as evidenced by the rcd1-1 anac017 double mutant showing partial suppression of rcd1 phenotypes including curly leaf morphology, MV tolerance, AOX abundance, MDS gene expression, and AOX respiration capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C53-C58 are well-supported by phenotypic observations (Figure 8A), chlorophyll fluorescence measurements (Figure 8B), immunoblotting (Figure 8C), qPCR (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and oxygen consumption measurements (Figure 8D). The partial suppression in the double mutant provides strong genetic evidence for RCD1's role as a negative regulator of ANAC017.

results.result: Background claims establishing the mechanistic context for organellar ROS signaling, including MV's mechanism of action, ROS formation and conversion in organelles, PAP metabolism and signaling, mitochondrial complex III ROS production, and ANAC013/ANAC017-mediated retrograde signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C65-C77 are supported by citations to established literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field. These provide the necessary context for interpreting the experimental results but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Background claims about prior work on RCD1, including its domain structure, interaction partners, mutant phenotypes, and previous characterization studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C85 are supported by citations to previous studies and provide context for the current work. These establish the foundation for investigating RCD1's role in organellar signaling but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Integrative model proposing that RCD1 functions as a nuclear integrator of chloroplast and mitochondrial signaling pathways, providing feedback control through ROS-sensitive regulation and negative regulation of ANAC013/ANAC017-mediated MDS gene expression. RCD1 is linked to PAP signaling and may primarily sense chloroplastic rather than mitochondrial ROS.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 and C61-C64 represent integrative conclusions and mechanistic interpretations. While these are reasonable inferences from the combined experimental evidence (RCD1-ANAC interactions, ROS sensitivity, transcriptomic overlaps, genetic interactions), they remain partially speculative. The model is well-supported by the data but would benefit from additional mechanistic validation.

results.result: Accumulating MDS gene products, including AOXs, affect chloroplast redox status, alter chloroplast ROS processing, and provide increased protection to the photosynthetic apparatus.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including altered 2-CP redox state (Figure 1C), increased AOX abundance and capacity (Figures 4A, 4C), different H2O2 production kinetics (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), SHAM effects on MV tolerance (Figure 4E), and increased PSII protection (Figure 1A, Figure 4D). The mechanistic connections are well-established through pharmacological and genetic manipulations.

results.result: RCD1 is a nuclear-localized transcriptional co-regulator.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by citations to previous studies (Jaspers et al., 2009; Jaspers et al., 2010a) and represents established knowledge about RCD1 that provides context for the current study.
